abstract: MRS-measured metabolite concentration estimates in the brain show significant changes over the lifespan. An important step in accurately quantifying metabolite levels using in vivo MRS is correction for T1- and T2- weighting of water and metabolite signals. Despite substantial literature indicating that both T1 and T2 of water and metabolites change across the lifespan, most aging studies use age-invariant reference values in quantification equations. It is important to establish whether observed changes in metabolite levels are driven by relaxation effects or actual concentration changes. In three recent studies, we have characterized changes in water and metabolite relaxation times across the adult lifespan, specifying linear models to predict age-appropriate T1 and T2 values for use in quantification. To establish whether prior metabolite-age correlation findings are driven by age-dependent errors in relaxation corrections, age-appropriate metabolite T1 and T2 values and age- and region-appropriate water T1 and T2 values were applied to re-calculate metabolite levels for a large lifespan cohort. While major metabolite (total N-acetyl aspartate tNAA, total choline tCho, total creatine tCr, myo-inositol mI, glutamate + glutamine Glx) concentration estimates were lower after using an age-appropriate relaxation correction analysis pipeline, the metabolite-age relationships were unchanged. We conclude that well-documented changes in metabolite and water relaxation times across the healthy adult lifespan do not drive findings of metabolite-age correlations.
